versions.body:
# Arithmetic update compatibility decision record

This was initially logged as an arithmetic update compatibility gap. The issue isn't whether a number can be written to a document field; it's that the numeric operation, extra attributes, and return value can't each follow different conventions. Callers will continue to use the result of an update; if the implementation splits a single call into two commits, the method name stays the same on the surface, but the result semantics have changed.

The starting point for locating the relevant code at the time was `src/Query/Builder.php`. The visible class was `Builder extends BaseBuilder`, so the issue was first discussed at the query builder layer. `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure` appear at the top of the file, indicating that this handles more than one simple kind of update call. The inheritance chain and the exact points where updates are assembled haven't been explored yet.

Two approaches were considered:

- Handle multiplication and division as separate operations, with another update for the extra attributes;
- For division, first switch to a reciprocal and reuse the multiplication path, keeping the extra attributes in the same update.

The second approach was the initial choice. The reason is that callers should receive the result of just one update. They shouldn't have to deal with two results just because they also supply extra attributes, or guess the call's status when the first step succeeds and the second fails. This is about the call boundary, not a claim that the database has no other ways to express the math.

Old note retained: division can be handled as a standalone database operator; the reciprocal is just a test formulation. No counterexample to this judgment has turned up yet, so leave it in. It naturally led early investigation toward a separate division branch and made "the attributes can be written afterward" look like an acceptable approach.

"Null values don't participate in arithmetic" was also just a brief note from that time. It didn't distinguish between a missing source field and a source field set to `null`, much less answer whether extra attributes could still be written when the numeric part was skipped. Whether the supplied multiplier or divisor itself needs a separate check was not explored in this record either.

Another point remains unresolved: when an extra attribute has the same name as the arithmetic target, is the policy to reject, overwrite, or let the actual update structure decide? The first draft only recorded the existence of this collision; the local snippets weren't sufficient to settle on any of these options.

The provisional decision is to prefer expressing division through the multiplication path and, by default, not split the numeric operation and extra attributes into two commits. Follow-up review should first confirm the conditions under which the source value participates, then check whether the object returned by a single call is still the original update result.
versions.change_summary: Recorded the reciprocal approach and two unresolved edge cases

versions.body:
# Arithmetic Update Compatibility Decision Record

This record originally contained only the conclusion "use a reciprocal for division." The review found that this sentence compressed three questions into one: whether the source value can participate in arithmetic, which update fragment includes the additional attributes, and what result the caller ultimately receives. Some readers still follow the old page's reference to a "standalone division operator" to look for an entry point, so the original judgment is retained. This revision only adds the boundaries that could be confirmed at the time.

## Direction Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft chose the "reciprocal plus multiplication" approach and kept the additional attributes and the numeric operation in the same call. This choice was about stability at the calling interface, not a claim about whether other mathematical operations exist underneath. If the numeric part and the attribute part are submitted separately, the caller receives more than one update result. If one part fails, there is also no natural single result representing the entire call.

The old note still says: division can be handled as a standalone database operator; using a reciprocal is just a way of writing it in tests.

That statement now reads as too sweeping, but it explains why the early investigation kept looking for a separate division branch, and why "add the additional attributes in a follow-up update" was once considered a reasonable suggestion. This review did not support that assumed entry point. The original sentence is retained to make the change in judgment visible.

## Scope of This Review

The investigation still points to `src/Query/Builder.php`. The namespace in the file is `MongoDB\Laravel\Query`, and the class is `Builder`, which extends `BaseBuilder`. This supports the judgment that "the arithmetic interface is part of the query builder's API surface," but it is not enough to attribute every update fragment to this class. Early notes conflated the file entry point with implementation ownership, leading later readers to treat a local code location as a complete map of responsibilities.

The file header includes `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure`. These are not direct evidence of arithmetic updates, but they highlight an easily overlooked fact: Builder handles arguments, callbacks, and different query shapes. Reading it as a thin wrapper for "multiply a field by a number" makes it easy to conflate argument issues, closure paths, and update structure.

This review added no runtime output. The review method was to lay out candidate behaviors by input shape and ask: what happens when the source value is unusable, whether the operation is still a single update when additional attributes are present, and whether the returned object is still the result of the existing update. Viewed this way, the earlier "division compatibility" question was not a single mathematical problem.

## Approaches Not Adopted

**Submitting field by field.** Update the numeric field first, then add the additional attributes. This is straightforward, but one call produces multiple results. If the first part succeeds and the second fails, the caller cannot determine what happened from a single return value. The early draft's suggestion to "send additional attributes through a separate update" is therefore no longer the default direction.

**Reading, then saving.** Retrieve the field's value, divide it by the supplied number in the application, then write the result back. This looks closest to the word "division," but it changes the operation boundary: the call is no longer a single action on the existing update path, but a combination of reading, computing, and saving. The old note described this idea as a standalone operator without distinguishing an underlying operator from an application-side workflow.

**Treating missing values as zero.** This suggestion was once made to keep the examples running smoothly. It turns "no usable source value" into a newly written number and conflates a missing value with an explicit `null`. This review concluded that it cannot serve as the default interpretation of arithmetic updates.

Another claim was that, as long as the numeric field is ultimately updated correctly, it does not matter whether the additional attributes are written in the same batch. The review did not accept this. It overlooks the caller-visible return value and mistakes "can be written" for "can be split up arbitrarily." Numeric values and attributes do not have to use the same update expression, but when they enter through the same Builder call, we cannot start by assuming that two results can substitute for one.

## Addendum on Source Values

The initial draft's "empty values do not participate in arithmetic" was too imprecise. After review, we started by splitting it into two working conclusions:

1. When the source field is missing, it cannot participate in multiplication or reciprocal-based arithmetic as an ordinary number.
2. When the source field is explicitly `null`, a numeric value cannot be generated automatically just because the caller supplied a multiplier or divisor.

These two conclusions concern only the source of the numeric value. They do not mean "the entire call does nothing," nor do they decide whether additional attributes are written. Several earlier discussions mixed these two layers together under "empty-value handling," leading some people to misread skipping the numeric operation as necessarily dropping the attributes too.

The supplied operation and the source field are two different kinds of objects. Even if the caller supplies a value usable for multiplication or a reciprocal, the source field may not be a usable source for a numeric update. Conversely, the existence of the source field does not establish, from this page, that all additional keys can be merged into the update unconditionally. With these distinctions in place, "empty value" in the old record is no longer treated as a term that covers every branch.

## Review Notes

Reviewers required that "mathematically equivalent" not be treated as "equivalent at the interface." Using a reciprocal is not just about writing one fewer branch. If division can follow the existing update's result semantics, callers do not have to take on an extra read, save, or second result just because the operation name changes.

Another comment concerned the additional attributes. They are not log fields added only after success; they are part of the same Builder call. This comment rejects splitting by default, not asserts that arbitrary keys with the same name can be merged unconditionally. How conflicting keys are handled still needs to be confirmed against the actual update structure.

The review also required retaining the old conclusion rather than rewriting it as though it had never appeared. The earlier idea of standalone division did help with the initial reading: it focused attention on the arithmetic operation itself. The problem was that it stopped there, without examining result boundaries or attribute writes. The later adjustment did not reject the initial focus on numeric values; it placed the numeric operation back in the context of a single update.

## Decision at This Revision

This revision narrows the direction to: prefer the multiplication update path for division; additional attributes should not get a separate update by default; missing values and `null` should not be passed off as numbers usable in arithmetic. This decision does not cover keys with the same name, complex field paths, or result wrapping in the inheritance chain.

For anyone still reading the old investigation, the order should change: first examine the numeric source and result of a single call, then check whether additional attributes enter the update along with it. Do not infer whether compatibility exists directly from "is there a standalone division branch?" That question can remain as a historical search term, but it is no longer the sole entry point for judging interface behavior.

# Arithmetic Update Compatibility Decision Record

This page gradually grew from a brief compatibility note into an entry point for earlier investigations. The earliest text called the issue "Arithmetic updates and reciprocal division", but later some read it as "whether a standalone division operator exists", while others judged whether additional attributes were handled solely by whether `$mul` appeared. Neither reading is sufficient, but they explain why this page retains many passages that no longer apply.

The entry point has always been `src/Query/Builder.php`. The file contains `namespace MongoDB\Laravel\Query;`, and declares `class Builder extends BaseBuilder`. This provides a location to refer back to: the discussion concerns arithmetic updates exposed by the query builder, not the model save flow. Early notes once turned "the entry point is in Builder" into "all update semantics are determined by Builder alone"; the latter was merely an inference intended to shorten the investigation path, and subsequent reviews did not retain it as a conclusion about responsibility.

At the time, the file header showed `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure`. These dependencies did not directly explain how multiplication, division, or attribute merging were implemented, but they made one fact clear: the parameter shapes and call paths this class handles extend far beyond a single arithmetic action. Several misreadings started here—first treating Builder as a single-purpose wrapper, then generalizing local observations into the complete set of update rules.

The page's old name also left a bias in how it was read. "reciprocal division" sounds as though it names an isolated mathematical approach, but the actual discussion had been asking from the outset: when a numeric action and additional attributes appear together, how many updates does the caller actually see, and what result do they get. The name has not changed because old reviews and old searches still use this term to find their way back here; the body no longer lets the name stand in for specific judgments.

---

## 2023-06-23: The Initial Trade-offs

The initial question was not "whether the database can perform division", but what should represent the result of a call when it includes both a numeric update and extra attributes. If the numeric fields are updated first and the attribute fields afterward, the caller has to deal with two return values. If the first step succeeds and the next step fails, the returned object also cannot naturally indicate whether the call as a whole counts as a success or a failure.

Two approaches were considered at the time.

The first was to make multiplication and division separate operations, with additional attributes submitted separately. This was easy to break apart for debugging: each field action had its own place, and it was also easy to find the corresponding branch from the word "division". The original notes even stated:

> Division can be handled as a standalone database operator, and the reciprocal is just test notation.

The second option was to rewrite division as multiplication by the reciprocal, and keep the properties that could be written together within a single update. The initial draft chose the second option. The decision at the time concerned only the call boundary: a single Builder call should not be split by default into two unrelated writes. It did not promise that all field combinations would work, nor did it explain how keys with the same name should be handled.

The initial draft also included the line "Null values do not participate in arithmetic". It is still clear today why that was insufficient. It squeezed the absence of the source field, a source field value of `null`, whether the supplied value was suitable for arithmetic, and whether the extra properties would still be written, all into the two-character term "null value". That was a risk marker, not a complete rule.

The issue left unresolved at the time was also very narrow: when an additional property and the arithmetic target collided on the same key, should it be rejected, overwritten, or left to the update structure itself to decide? The initial draft did not contain a snippet concrete enough to settle this debate, so the early "leaning toward rejection" should not be treated as behavior that was later confirmed.

Another concern in the initial draft was the calling interface rather than field names. If a method returned one update result for the numeric operation but returned another result for the extra properties, the caller would have to decide which one to trust. If only the latter result were returned, the numeric operation would be obscured; if only the former result were returned, the property operation would be obscured instead. This issue was not described as a "return-value boundary" in the early stages, but it was already a practical reason for choosing the reciprocal approach.

---

## Marginal notes on the old meeting minutes

In the first discussion, some people supported a separate division approach not because it had already been shown to be more appropriate, but because it seemed easier to locate. Looking for a corresponding handling point when seeing "divide" is a natural reading step; putting property updates in a separate section also made each section look shorter. The brief post-meeting note did not object to this reading order, but only cautioned against inferring from it that two writes were still equivalent to a single interface call.

Another question left unresolved at the time was what exactly "extra properties" meant. The early wording made them sound like trailing supplementary information, as though writing them after the numeric operation was complete would have no impact. This description later proved prone to misinterpretation. It did not explain which call the properties came in through, nor whether the properties also had to disappear when the numeric portion was skipped because the source value was unavailable. The old notes have no answer, and they are being retained to avoid disguising questions that had not been properly clarified at the time as rules that had already been decided.

The statement "Get the numeric changes right first, and deal with the result object later" also came up during the meeting. That was a temporary ordering of priorities, not a decision. For callers using Builder, the result object is not just for recordkeeping; once the interface splits a single operation apart, the caller's understanding of what happened during that call is split apart as well. Subsequent reviews took this very gap as their starting point in calling for the problem to be reframed.

---

## 2023-10-23: Someone looked in the wrong place using the old terminology

During the second pass, the old notes were still influencing the investigation. Someone started with "reciprocal division" and looked for a separately named division entry point; after failing to find one, they interpreted the problem as compatibility not having been implemented yet. This path seemed consistent with the literal wording, but it did not answer the real interface question: whether division could still retain the result semantics of a single update.

The review instead started from the shape of the input. Whether the numeric source can participate in the operation, how additional attributes enter the update, and how the underlying result returns to the caller are three related but non-interchangeable questions. Previously, grouping them all under "division compatibility" caused the discussion to keep circling back to the same term without making progress.

There was no new runtime output at that point. What remained was a small set of judgments: when the source field is absent, it should not be treated as zero out of thin air; when the source field is explicitly `null`, it also cannot automatically produce a numeric value just because the caller provides a multiplier or divisor. This refers only to the numeric source; it does not mean the call as a whole must necessarily be a no-op. Earlier, some people read "skip the numeric value" directly as "additional attributes cannot be written either," but there was no basis for that at the time.

The same review also revisited Builder's local role. `Builder extends BaseBuilder` can support the claim that "the interface is on the query-builder surface," but the full division of responsibilities among the parent class, subclass, and underlying driver cannot be inferred from the inheritance declaration. The file entry point is a navigation aid, not a complete implementation map. That record did not lay out the inheritance chain segment by segment, not because it was unimportant, but because the question at the time was still at the level of whether a single update should be split apart.

During the review, "missing" and "explicit `null`" were written separately—not to create different mathematical rules for them, but to prevent the old approach from turning both into zero. Missing means there is no field available as a numeric source; `null` means the field already has an explicit null value. Neither case can automatically produce a numeric value merely because the call itself has already been specified. This judgment only constrains the numeric part; it cannot be expanded into a negation of all other update keys.

Some also suggested ending the entire call immediately when the numeric part could not proceed. That suggestion did not make it into the decision at the time, because it tied together again two layers that had not yet been separated: whether the numeric source can participate and how additional attributes are represented in the same update are not the same judgment. The review therefore did not confirm any attribute-conflict rules; it only rejected using the source field's null state as a substitute for all subsequent judgments.

---

## Review note: Equivalent numbers are not necessarily equivalent interfaces

A review addendum did not try to rewrite the original decision; it only asked that the "reciprocal" direction be made explicit. If the implementation were changed to read the current field value, compute on the application side, and then save, the final number might be the same as with a direct update, but the operation boundary would have changed: it would introduce a read point and a save step, and might no longer return the same kind of underlying result.

The review therefore supported retaining the reciprocal direction. This support was not a line-by-line approval of a particular expression, but a judgment about interface risk: the caller should not have to additionally take on a read, a save, or two result objects merely because it uses division. The reciprocal is not intended to make the code look more mathematical, but to avoid turning division into a different kind of call.

Another note addressed additional attributes. They are not side-channel information to be written only after the main update succeeds; since they are supplied by the same call, they cannot by default be scheduled as a second submission. What the review rejected was the default "compute first, then fill in" plan, not a claim that arbitrary keys can be mixed together without conflict. The earlier draft overstated this point; that wording was later withdrawn.

One reviewer summarized it at the time: do not substitute "mathematically equivalent" for "interface-equivalent." This sentence was often quoted later, but it cannot by itself determine conflicts between specific keys. It only explains why the old read—compute—save approach is no longer preferred.

The review also asked for a more specific explanation of "the same call". It does not mean that all fields must use the same operation, nor does it mean that each fragment produces its own independent result. Numeric actions and additional attributes can play different roles; what must be preserved is that they are not split into two API operations by default just because the method name changes from multiplication to division. This addendum corrects the sequence of the earlier troubleshooting, and does not establish a separate general-purpose update model.

---

## A revised position after one experiment

An early proposal leaned toward treating division as a separate operation. The following passage is retained as a working idea from that time and is no longer recommended:

> First retrieve the current field value, divide it by the input number on the application side, then save it; if attributes are also included, perform another update after success. Each step is easy to debug.

The reason it was later rejected was not that "easy to debug" was wrong, but that it changed the meaning of a single update. It first reads the current value, then writes the numeric value back; the additional attributes may in turn become a second action. As a result, the return value and concurrency timing no longer naturally follow the existing multiplication approach.

Another rejected idea was this: when the source field is missing, fill in zero first, then continue with the arithmetic. This idea was once used to get isolated examples to work, but it turned "no source value available to participate" into a new numeric value and also erased the distinction between a missing value and an explicit `null`. The later write-up did not adopt it.

This change in position did not introduce a new overarching principle, but only narrowed the previous guidance: do not piece together a read—calculate—save workflow on the application side just to obtain a numeric result; and do not invent an initial value for a missing value just to keep the path executing.

The post-experiment notes also preserved an easily overlooked distinction: implementing division separately does not necessarily cause an immediate numeric error; what it changes first is the shape of the API. A check that only compares the final field value is very likely to miss that reading, calculating, writing back, and the follow-up attribute write already constitute a different sequence of operations. The old example therefore cannot be justified again on the grounds that "the result is the same".

Likewise, the old zero-filling example is not merely a default-value choice. It turns a case that originally had no numeric source into one with a numeric result, then continues processing it using multiplication or a reciprocal. The number obtained this way does not prove that the original field participated in the arithmetic, but instead conceals the point at which source-value filtering should have occurred. This example is retained in the appendix, and is no longer used as a troubleshooting example.

---

## Four layers left in the margins

In later discussions, the issues were temporarily recorded separately to avoid calling every problem "division" again. This categorization is not new API terminology, just an order for reading the old notes.

**Numeric target.** The field targeted by the multiplication or reciprocal approach is the primary target of this arithmetic action. The primary target is not an alias for the additional attributes, nor should it be silently replaced by other keys in the same call.

**Numeric source.** Calculation can continue only if the source value exists and can participate in the numeric action. Neither a missing value nor `null` should be passed off as zero; this layer only states whether the numeric part participates, and does not replace the assessment of other attributes.

**Additional attributes.** Calling Fang Ke allows non-numeric attributes to be included in the same call. They are not a reason to trigger a second update, but a different type of problem arises when they have the same name as the numeric target. The old page did not retain enough isolated examples, so the early leaning is not used here to fill in a uniform handling approach.

**Result.** A single call should continue to return the result produced by the underlying update. This is the earliest reason for rejecting the splitting of the operation, and the reason the read–calculate–save approach was later no longer adopted.

Once the four layers are separated, several old misreadings become clearer. Checking only whether `$mul` appears can show only that the numeric update fragment exists; it cannot, by itself, explain how additional properties enter the same operation. Seeing only that a source value is empty also cannot directly establish that all additional properties are discarded. Collapsing these different questions into one statement—"the arithmetic update is problematic"—would cause subsequent investigation to start from the wrong entry point.

This layering also explains why the Builder file header cannot directly serve as proof of behavior. `ArgumentCountError` and `BadMethodCallException` remind readers that the interface is not without irregular forms, `Closure` reminds them that the call surface includes a callback form, and `Carbon\CarbonPeriod` further shows that the processing objects near this class are not all numeric fields. They do not provide the final semantics of the arithmetic update, but they are sufficient to refute the reading that "as long as you see Builder, you can collapse all problems into a single numeric branch."

In an earlier review, some people conflated the concepts of a "numeric target" and a "numeric source" as the same field concept: they assumed that the existence of a target meant that a computable source value could be obtained. Others focused only on additional properties, believing that a writable property necessarily meant that the numeric portion was also valid. Both confusions skip the conditions that actually need to be checked. The value of layering is not that it adds terminology, but that it makes these leaps identifiable.

---

## Three Shortcuts We Did Not Continue Using

**Per-field submission.** Update the numeric field first, then add the additional properties. This makes each action easy to observe separately, but causes a single Builder call to expose multiple results. If one action fails, the caller cannot determine the overall outcome of the call from a single returned object. This approach appeared in the first draft as a readability suggestion; it is no longer the default implementation direction.

**Read then save.** First obtain the current field value, divide it by the supplied number on the application side, and then write the result back. In wording, it is closest to "division," but it turns the original update direction into a combination of reading, calculating, and saving. Even if the final number is the same, the call boundary, result semantics, and timing are all different.

**Treat missing values as zero.** This makes it easier for local examples to proceed, but turns a field with no source into a new numeric value and merges missingness with `null` into the same state. This shortcut does not resolve whether the source value should participate in the arithmetic; instead, it bypasses that question.

The three shortcuts have one thing in common: not that "they can never write a number," but that they all make the early interface issues invisible: a single update is split into several, a source value that should not have participated is artificially filled in, or the final result is treated as the only criterion. These failed approaches are retained so that people reading the old investigation later will know which statements can no longer be used.

---

## Additional Note After Excerpts from the Old Review

One review narrowed the dispute to two questions: whether division still falls within the existing update approach, and whether it causes extra attributes to become a follow-up operation. This framing is more useful than "whether division is supported", because the latter only directs readers to look for a named branch. The review did not call for resolving all key conflicts immediately, nor did it argue that Builder alone should bear full responsibility for the implementation.

Another reviewer asked that file paths not be treated as conclusions. `src/Query/Builder.php` is the reference location for this page, and `Builder` is the object whose interface surface is under discussion; what further reading from here reveals depends on the actual update structure and inheritance path. The statement in the early notes that "all the logic is here" has been struck out. The paths are retained so that earlier questions can be traced back to the same local entry point, not to expand that entry point into the full map.

Together, these two review comments changed how the record is written: first state what a single call must preserve, then explain why using the reciprocal stays closer to that boundary than read—compute—save; first state that source values should not be fabricated, then separate judgments about attributes from judgments about the sources of numeric values. The old paragraphs were not deleted, because they remain the reason the early review favored a standalone operator.

---

## 2025-03-12: The current position is added after the earlier record

This round did not delete the earlier language about "standalone division", but explicitly corrected it afterward. What needs to be confirmed now is not whether a division operation can be simulated manually, but whether these two Builder interfaces maintain the same kind of update boundary, the same kind of return value, and the same kind of source-value filtering at the compatibility entry points.

Query\Builder::multiply performs a synchronous numeric $mul update, merges optional extra attributes under $set, excludes missing or null source values, and Query\Builder::divide delegates with the reciprocal; both return the underlying update result.

This requirement retracts several overly vague earlier statements. The numeric update is synchronous; optional extra attributes go under `$set`; source values that are missing or `null` do not participate in the numeric update; division delegates using the reciprocal; both paths return the underlying update result. This is not about renaming every past conjecture, but about clearly defining the scope of behavior that can be used for current verification.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Source Value Check" as source_check
    state "Reciprocal Delegation" as reciprocal
    state "Numeric Update ($mul)" as multiply
    state "Optional Additional Attributes ($set)" as extras
    state "Skip Numeric Part" as skipped
    state "Underlying Update Result" as result

    [*] --> source_check
    source_check --> multiply: Multiplication
    source_check --> reciprocal: Division
    reciprocal --> multiply: reciprocal
    source_check --> skipped: missing or null
    multiply --> extras
    skipped --> extras
    extras --> result
```

"Skip Numeric Part" in the diagram must not be expanded into "the entire call has no changes." It only means that the source value does not participate in the numeric operation when it is missing or equals `null`. Whether optional attributes exist, whether they conflict with the numeric target, and whether they themselves are writable are separate questions.

Likewise, `$set` is not a synonym for a post hoc patch. It indicates that optional additional attributes and `$mul` serve different expressive roles, yet appear in the same update. The earlier approach was abandoned not because additional attributes were unimportant, but precisely because splitting them into a second write would change the result boundary of a single call.

"divide delegates with the reciprocal" also retracts the draft's description that "the reciprocal is merely test syntax." Here, the reciprocal is not a technique that the caller must precompute in advance, but the delegation method of `Query\Builder::divide`. It avoids implementing division as a separate path that first reads the current record, then calculates on the application side, and then saves.

The current wording also makes the old return-value statement verifiable. What is required here is not to manually assemble a return object that merely appears identical, but for both Builder paths to return the underlying update result. This way, multiplication and division do not expose two-stage results to the caller merely because their internal mathematical expressions differ, nor turn a single numeric operation into the output of a read workflow.

The requirement for synchronous numeric updates also limits how the old examples apply. It does not allow "a number was eventually written back" to be treated as sufficient, because reading, then calculating, then saving is no longer the synchronous update approach used here. Application-side calculations in the old approach can still serve as material for explaining earlier misjudgments, but cannot replace the current delegation of multiplication or reciprocals.

---

## Questions Still on the Sidelines

When an additional property has the same name as a numeric target, this page does not make the final ruling. What can be confirmed is the responsibilities of `$mul` and `$set`, and that they are part of a single update; when the two fragments point to the same key, the earlier "inclination to reject" cannot stand in for the actual handling.

Complex field paths are another adjacent issue. The early draft assumed that a "field" meant the simplest kind of top-level key, and that example is not sufficient to cover other path forms. If an investigation starts with a specific field, first determine whether its source value meets the numeric conditions described here, then inspect the update structure that Builder actually produces.

The presence of `BaseBuilder` still serves only as a navigation aid. It reminds readers that the returned result may come from beyond the local class, but this does not justify attributing unexamined superclass behavior to the arithmetic decisions on this page. The old record relied too heavily on the file entry point; the new version no longer follows that attribution method.

Argument exceptions and callback forms are also outside the scope of this decision. `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, and `Closure` appear in adjacent parts of the file, which only indicates that readers of Builder should not assume that all calls have the same argument shape. They cannot, in turn, be used as evidence of behavior involving multiplication, division, or property conflicts.

The unresolved items do not weaken what has already been established. There is already a current position on numeric filtering when the source value is missing or is `null`, delegation using reciprocals, the division of responsibilities between `$mul` and `$set`, and returning the underlying update result. Key conflicts and complex paths still need to be verified against the actual update structure; decisions that were never recorded should not be invented just to make this old page look complete.

---

## Appendix: Two Old Examples

**Old example one: Fill in missing source values with zero.** An early draft suggested first initializing fields with no value to zero, then continuing the calculation. This example later became inapplicable because it turned a missing value into an additional write and also obscured the distinction between a missing value and `null`. It is retained to explain why "empty values do not participate in arithmetic" cannot be read as an initialization rule.

This old example also created a misleading impression: the eventual appearance of a numeric value in the sample was taken as evidence that the source field had participated in the calculation. In fact, the numeric value might have come from a preliminary write rather than the original source. The current position rules out this interpretation, so the old example can only be used to understand the earlier judgment, not to verify current behavior.

**Old example 2: Read the value, then divide, then save.** The earlier draft assumed that as long as the final number was correct, division could be split into a read, application-side computation, and a save. This example later became inapplicable because it departed from reciprocal delegation and did not preserve the way the underlying update result is returned. It was once a reasonable working assumption, but should no longer be treated as an example of the current interface.

This example remained undeleted for so long because it accurately exposed the priorities at the time: first find a mathematical process that was easy to explain, then check the interface result. Only when a later review reversed that order did it become clear that read—compute—save could not replace a single synchronous update. The old example is retained not to keep it available as a fallback, but to make this change in position traceable.

**Old example 3: Write attributes after success.** Early discussions treated additional attributes as a trailing action that did not affect the numeric update, and therefore recommended making another submission after the numeric write was complete. This example is no longer applicable. It would split a single Builder call into two parts and force the caller to decide for themselves between two results. The current guidance requires optional extra attributes to be placed in `$set`, and no longer follows the default "write after success" path.

This record retains earlier judgments, review annotations, and overturned proposals because they still explain why earlier investigations began with "standalone division". Current verification should follow the 2025-03-12 guidance; to understand why earlier code reviews took a roundabout route, start with the earlier layers of the timeline.

# Vector Interface Compatibility Proposal

First, distinguish the two names: `Unsupported vector distance API` means the distance interface itself is not accepted by the current compatibility layer; `Vector search auto-embedding` concerns whether vectors are generated on the caller's behalf before vector search. The initial assessment was that they might share a Builder entry point, so we could first observe failures in the same place, then decide whether to introduce a conversion.

The code location we can point to directly at this stage is `src/Query/Builder.php`. The file declares the `MongoDB\\Laravel\\Query` namespace, and `Builder` (line 88) inherits from `BaseBuilder`; the file also imports `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure` at the top. These details are enough to establish this as a local entry point for the query builder, but not enough to prove that it already implements vector distance parameters or automatic embedding.

Candidate approaches:

- Preserve the distance expression supplied by the caller, and fail explicitly at the Builder for unsupported forms. This avoids silently changing the meaning of the query, but requires callers to prepare acceptable vectors themselves.
- Add a compatibility conversion at the Builder. This keeps the caller-facing surface relatively small, but we must first confirm every type of distance expression and when vectors are generated; otherwise, errors will be deferred from the interface layer to query execution.
- Put automatic embedding before query construction, so the Builder only receives vectors that are already prepared. This gives us a clearer boundary, but requires finding another existing automation entry point.

None of these can be recorded as a decision yet. First, use the maintainers' usual release command to check where the failure occurs, then confirm the downloadable artifacts; next, trigger the job for automatic embedding through an existing automation entry point in the repository, recording the job, commit, and actual artifact name. Until the review results come back, the provisional withdrawal condition is: do not submit a conversion that cannot distinguish distance interface failures from vector generation failures.

# Vector Interface Compatibility Plan

Early records handled two issues through the same Builder entry point. This was a working hypothesis that made it easier to start the investigation and should not continue to be treated as a design premise. `Unsupported vector distance API` concerns whether the distance capability already supplied by the call is accepted; `Vector search auto-embedding` concerns whether a vector has been generated before the query. The former can fail at the parameter boundary; the latter also involves the generation step, job entry point, and artifact record. Combining them into a single "compatibility conversion" makes the failure location unclear and hides undecided async or upstream behavior inside the query builder.

## Code Location

The file we can currently verify is `src/Query/Builder.php`. The declaration at the top is:

```php
namespace MongoDB\\Laravel\\Query;
```

Near line 88 is:

```php
class Builder extends BaseBuilder
```

The direct dependencies listed in the file header include `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure`. This can serve as an inspection point for the query builder, but the available location material does not identify vector distance methods, an automatic embedding function, or their callers. Accordingly, this proposal does not infer implementation ownership from the file location, nor treat the presence of a name as evidence that the interface is already available.

## Candidate Splits

**A: Builder only performs a boundary check for distance support.** Callers continue to provide the vector and distance expression; Builder immediately fails on unsupported distance forms and retains the original input for troubleshooting. This is the easiest direction for preserving query semantics, but callers must know which distance forms are supported. It does not solve automatic embedding on its own, because the vector may not exist yet when Builder receives the request.

**B: Builder performs parameter compatibility conversion.** The same entry point maps the caller's distance parameters to an expression the current driver can handle and, when necessary, triggers vector preparation. The changes appear localized, but this risks conflating three kinds of error: an invalid distance expression, vector generation failure, and a generated result not making it into the actual query. If it is not possible to record a result at each stage, automatic conversion should not be adopted by default.

**C: Upstream completes automatic embedding first; Builder only consumes the result.** Automatic embedding is handled by the existing automation entry point, and the query builder receives only the prepared vector and distance parameters. This separates "what to generate" from "how to query"; migration requires confirming that the existing job can leave a record of the job, commit, and actual artifact name, and requires callers to accept the new preparation order. The material currently available does not confirm this entry point, so C is an option awaiting validation, not a finalized architecture.

The early draft leaned toward choosing between A and B. After review, the more appropriate comparison is whether the "distance interface" and "vector preparation" chains can fail independently and roll back independently. Even if the same file ultimately handles the request, that does not mean the two chains should be written as one success condition.

## Trial Records and Known Gaps

LMC-222 left the following check: use the release command the maintainer uses day to day to check "Unsupported vector distance API", and record the failing phase and downloadable artifact separately. There is no actual command output yet, so we cannot fill in whether the failure occurred during build, release, or runtime. LMC-228 left the following check: from the repository's existing automation entry point, trigger the job corresponding to "Vector search auto-embedding", and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name. There is likewise no job result, so automatic embedding cannot be described as having run or succeeded.

Once both records are complete, they should at minimum answer three questions: when the distance interface is evaluated after the call enters Builder; whether vector generation occurs before or after query construction; and whether a query is still sent when generation fails. If the third question has no clear answer, B cannot serve as the compatibility default. The "interface unsupported" and "no vector obtained" cases must also be kept as two separately identifiable failure records, so the release check does not leave only one generic vector-search failure.

## Migration and Rollback

With A, migration cost falls mainly on callers: existing users must prepare the vector in advance and determine the supported range before choosing a distance form. With C, migration cost falls on the automation entry point and call order: run the generation job first, then pass the actual artifact and commit information into the query. With B, the migration appears smallest, but if the conversion rules are incomplete, a callerFang Ke can receive an incorrect query without any obvious indication, and rollback cost is highest.

The recommendation at this stage is to test A first and treat C as a separate automatic-embedding experiment; B should enter implementation discussion only after the distance expressions, generation timing, and failure records can each be checked independently. On rollback, do not retain unverified automatic conversion: remove the conversion and return to explicitly passing the vector or explicitly reporting unsupported distance forms. The following remain undecided: which distance expressions are supported, the exact name of the automation entry point, how the artifact is handed to the query builder, and whether a compatibility failure needs to preserve the old calling convention. Until review results are available for the items above, do not present the plan as a release commitment.

# Sorting Compatibility Troubleshooting Tree

After an upgrade, if you encounter a sorting difference, first split the situation into two areas: the direction value passed in by the caller and the sort order rewritten by chunked reads to continue paging. Both are near `src/Query/Builder.php`, but they should not be treated as the same kind of failure.

At the time, the investigation started by tracing string-based calls. When you see `asc` or `desc`, retain the original value and confirm whether it reaches Builder; don't perform another conversion at the call site first and then guess from the result what Builder did. The `Builder` in the file is in the `MongoDB\Laravel\Query` namespace and inherits from `BaseBuilder`; when you need to verify the sort shape, you can start here.

```text
Sorting anomaly
├─ Anomaly occurs when calling orderBy
│  └─ Record the direction value passed in
└─ First chunk reads normally; order changes in the next chunk
   └─ Record the complete sort order before rewriting
```

Older records described chunked reads as "append an id at the end." This wording is sufficient only for the simplest sample. If the original sort has a second element, you cannot determine whether the original order is still present by looking only at the last field.

At this stage, keep the field-name/direction pairs, such as `score => -1`, rather than first normalizing them to consecutive numeric indices. If you only have the final sort order, or cannot tell which of `id` and `_id` came from the previous read, stop at the original object position; do not continue deleting fields.

To be added: the actual shape of the direction object after it enters Builder; whether chunked reads use `id` or `_id`; the order of existing and newly added items when a second sort already exists.

# Sort compatibility troubleshooting tree

This record initially categorized post-upgrade sorting issues as "direction values are no longer strings." On review, that category was too narrow: some calls behaved abnormally as soon as they entered `orderBy`; for others, the first chunk read normally, but from the next chunk onward the results no longer followed the original query's order. Both symptoms can occur in a single upgrade, but their investigation records must not be mixed.

## The old entry point remains; the old check is no longer enough

The early guidance was: if you see a non-string direction, convert it to `asc` or `desc` and try again. This once made old calls appear stable again, so it was treated as a temporary troubleshooting measure. That guidance should now be retained as a historical record: it only shows that the old calls depended on the string path, not that other forms of direction values are inherently problematic.

In `src/Query/Builder.php`, you can locate `MongoDB\Laravel\Query\Builder`, declared as `class Builder extends BaseBuilder`. When investigating sort compatibility, you can start here to check where values sit relative to sort objects; the file header also includes dependencies such as `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure`, which must not all be interpreted as clues about pagination handling.

## Collect the objects before following the branches

Keep at least three things in every report: the direction value passed by the call, the associative sort before chunking starts, and the fields that must be appended to continue reading. An associative sort is a structure in which field names and direction values are still stored as pairs, for example:

```text
priority => -1
id       => 1
name     => 1
```

It is not a plain list ordered by 0, 1, and 2. This distinction determines whether you can tell that the old id entry is really gone, and whether an unrelated secondary sort gets deleted by mistake.

```text
Sort or next-page results look wrong
│
├─ Already wrong when calling orderBy
│  ├─ Argument is still asc / desc
│  │  └─ Leave it unchanged; inspect the direction after Builder
│  └─ Argument is not one of the original strings
│     └─ Record the original value; do not rewrite it before assessing it
│
└─ Only wrong when continuing to read
   ├─ The associative sort before rewriting is available
   │  ├─ Find the field used for the previous page continuation
   │  ├─ Record the other sort entries individually
   │  └─ Compare the field–direction pairs after rewriting
   └─ Only a numeric list or final results remain
      └─ Stop; go back to before the sort was rewritten
```

This stop condition does not mean the problem is solved. It prevents guesses from being written back into the sort object. Looking only for an id at the end of the final results cannot tell you whether it is an old entry, a newly appended entry, or a field the caller originally requested.

## A check that wasn't clearly explained

During review, someone treated the existing sort as a plain list: delete the last element that looks like id, then put the requested field at the end. Single-field samples did not immediately expose a problem, so this approach was retained for a while. For objects with a secondary sort, position is not enough to identify the entry: the last entry might not be a page-continuation entry at all, and deleting it would break the original query. Even if id is still visible at the end, that does not confirm whether previous entries have been left behind.

Another approach was to clear the sort and append only the page-continuation field. This avoided obvious duplication of old entries but dropped the other ordering carried by the original query. For samples read using only a single field, this loss was not obvious; when a secondary sort is present, the next chunk of results may no longer reflect the original query's intent.

So you cannot arbitrarily choose between "delete the last entry" and "clear and re-add." First confirm that the object still retains an associative mapping, then identify which entry belongs to the previous page continuation. Only then is there a basis for further action.

## 2023 year-end addendum

`id` and `_id` must be recorded verbatim. Calling both "primary key" makes later comparisons meaningless. Record each of the following: which field this read requires; which field appeared before rewriting; and, if both fields appear, which one can be confirmed as coming from the previous read.

The sequence recorded at the time was: retain the original associative sort; find the old page-continuation field; do not change any unrelated secondary sort; finally, check whether the new field is already present. The first version did not answer how to tell the two apart when "a field with the same name could come from either the original query or page continuation," so you should still stop when you encounter that structure rather than delete entries in bulk by name.

## Old passage that has been corrected

> When reading in chunks, append id directly to the end of the sort; if id is already present, the other fields are not affected.

This is an old procedure and is no longer a step to follow. It did not distinguish between `id` and `_id`, nor did it require preserving the relationship between field names and direction values. Later records quoting this passage should label it as old guidance, not quietly rewrite it into a new conclusion.

## Investigation note format

A record can be brief:

```text
Original direction value: ……
Before chunking: priority => -1, id => 1, name => 1
Suspected old page-continuation entry: id
Field for this read: _id
After chunking: ……
```

If there is no secondary sort, state that explicitly. If you cannot identify where the old entry came from, write "unidentified" and retain the original object. Do not invent fields just to fill out the structure.

# Sorting Compatibility Troubleshooting Tree

Sorting compatibility reports often contain only one sentence: the direction value cannot be passed through, or after chunked reading, the order does not match the original query. In the field, do not change fields directly based on this sentence. First determine whether the anomaly occurs when calling `orderBy`, or after continued reading takes over the existing sort; the former concerns translation of the direction value, while the latter concerns how the sort object is replaced.

This page retains old records, margin notes, and handling that was corrected later. Some judgments in earlier paragraphs are already obsolete but remain in place—not so that people will follow them, but because old issue tickets and screenshots once described the situation using those terms. Start routine troubleshooting with the flow below; when you need to explain an old result, review the dated records.

## First break down the situation

Before starting, record three things: the direction value passed to the call, the complete sort before chunked reading begins, and the fields that continued reading is required to use. If any one of the three is missing, do not infer the rewrite process from the last field in the final output.

```text
Sorting or chunked-reading result is abnormal
│
├─ Immediate exception when calling orderBy
│  │
│  ├─ Parameter is still asc / desc
│  │  └─ Retain the original string and verify the direction after Builder processing
│  │
│  └─ Parameter is not the original string
│     └─ Record the original value and call site; do not convert it in the caller first
│
└─ First segment is normal; anomaly occurs only when reading the next segment
   │
   ├─ The pre-rewrite associated sort is still available
   │  ├─ Mark the old continuation-page fields
   │  ├─ List the unrelated secondary sort separately
   │  └─ Compare the rewritten field–direction pairs
   │
   └─ Only a numeric-index list or the final sort remains
      └─ Stop; return to the object from before the sort was rewritten
```

Here, the associated sort is a mapping that stores field names and direction values in pairs, for example `score => -1`. It is not the same structure as an ordinary list stored under incrementing indices such as 0, 1, and 2. As long as the field name remains, you can determine whether an item is an old continuation-page item, the caller's original sort, or a newly appended field; as long as the direction value remains paired with the field, you can determine whether the secondary sort was changed accidentally.

The direction branch and the chunking branch can occur in the same call, but they cannot serve as proof of each other. If the direction has the expected numeric value while the continuation sort still retains an old item, the problem is sort replacement; if the continuation sort has the expected shape while the direction value was already rewritten before reaching Builder, return to the call entry point. Do not change the object in the other branch just to fix one branch.

## 2023-05-24: Initial record

The initial version had to handle existing calls that still passed `asc`, `desc`, so the record focused on whether strings could enter Builder. The shorthand at the time was: keep string directions as they are; if a non-string value was encountered, convert it to a string first and try again.

This guidance explains why the old calls appeared stable. They were originally on the string path, and manual conversion might not reveal any additional difference. But this does not mean that the non-string direction itself should be rewritten by the caller. The old records did not preserve the original shape of the direction object, nor distinguish between "the interface does not recognize the value" and "the investigator changed the value too early."

The same initial record described chunked reads as "append id at the end." At the time, this wording applied only to the simplest single-field read; it did not explain how the original ordering was preserved, nor whether existing sort items might have come from the previous continuation page. It was the first conclusion on this page to be overturned later.

When local code needs to be read, the entry point is still `src/Query/Builder.php`. The visible declaration is `class Builder extends BaseBuilder` under the `MongoDB\Laravel\Query` namespace. This location is sufficient to help inspect nearby locations related to sorting; it does not mean that all behavior in the file belongs to this issue.

## 2023-05-25: Review margin note

After the initial draft review, a short reminder was left in the margin: a direction is a translation of a value; a continuation page is a replacement of the sort object. Both may appear together with `orderBy`, but they should not be patched in the same place.

This note was later used to identify two types of misjudgment. The first treated a non-string direction directly as an unknown direction, thus changing the parameter at the caller first; this would hide the actual compatibility surface in a temporary conversion. The second saw an id at the end of the chunked result and concluded that the ordering was correct; the presence of one field does not show that the old alias has been removed, nor that the earlier secondary sort is still there.

The review did not provide the full rule here; it left only one clear stopping point: when the associated sort order from before the rewrite is unavailable, do not infer what happened from the last item in the final list. Return to the point where the field name and direction value still appear as a pair, and continue from there.

The file header shows dependencies such as `ArgumentCountError`, `BadMethodCallException`, `Carbon\CarbonPeriod`, and `Closure`. Early on, someone followed these imports to look for a "pagination handler," and ultimately mistook an unrelated call for the place where sorting was rewritten. Since then, the convention on this page has been to save the actual sort object first, then use file locations to aid reading; do not infer the runtime path from every symbol in the file.

## 2023-11-10: Where the recheck failed

During the second pass of cleanup, the object under review began to include a secondary sort. The initial approach treated the existing sort as an ordinary list: remove the last element that looked like an id, then put the field from the current request at the end. Single-field samples did not fail immediately, so it was once mistakenly considered usable.

The object below shows why this approach is insufficient:

```text
score => -1
id    => 1
name  => 1
```

If the deletion is done by position, the last item might be `name` rather than the old `id`. Even if an id is still visible in the output, there is no way to tell whether it is an item left over from the original or an item appended later. Whether the sort directions of `score` and `name` are still preserved also cannot be inferred from "an id is present at the end".

At the time, another attempt was to clear the entire sort and then append only the pagination field. It did not leave an obvious old id, but it also wiped out the other sorts from the original query. When reading only by id, this damage was not easy to notice; when `score`, `name`, or another unrelated ordering was present, the next chunk read no longer followed the original query.

The conclusion from this review was: you cannot simply choose between "delete the last item" and "clear and add". Both approaches treat the sort structure as positional. First confirm that the original object is still an associative mapping from field names to direction values, then confirm the old pagination field; only after that can replacement be discussed.

This pass also unpacked a seemingly simple term. `id` and `_id` cannot both be uniformly called a "primary key" in the record. During troubleshooting, write down separately: the field name in the original sort, the field name requested this time, and the field name that can be confirmed as belonging to the previous read. Whether the two names are the same or different, deletion cannot be determined solely from similarity between the names.

## Old operation: append-at-end method

> For chunked reads, append id directly to the end of the sort. If id is already present, other fields are not affected.

This passage was retained from the original operating instructions and is now deprecated. It did not distinguish whether the existing `id` was a sort originally requested by the caller or an alias left by the previous page read; it also did not handle `_id`, much less require that the sort continue to remain an associative mapping.

If old scripts or old screenshots still show "append id at the end", treat it only as a description of the historical state. Do not try to fix it by adding another field to the current object; that would mix the leftover item with the item appended this time in the same result, making it harder later to explain which came from where.

## 2025-02-04: Walking back the old conclusion

The latest revision formally split direction mapping and chunked-read replacement into two checkpoints. This is not because they are necessarily triggered by different code paths, but because the two types of results require different raw material: direction issues require preserving the input value and the result of processing it; continuation-page issues require preserving the associative sort order before and after rewriting.

This revision also explicitly rejected the "having an id is enough" check. For chunked reads, what matters is not whether some similarly named field appears in the final output, but whether the field previously used for continuation pages has been removed from the map, whether an unrelated secondary sort is still present, and whether the current request's field has been appended as the new continuation sort order. If an intermediate step has already converted the object into a numerically indexed list, first return to the point before that conversion; do not relabel a numeric list as an associative sort order.

The meeting notes retain a counterexample: when there is a secondary sort in addition to the primary sort, appending to the end does not prove that the secondary sort is still preserved. This counterexample is enough to refute the old conclusion based on "checking only the last field". The meeting did not require all calls to use the same sort order, nor did it require all direction values to be converted by the caller; it required the captured records to distinguish between the two checkpoints.

## Current Direction Verification

Stop using the old approach of "converting non-strings to strings first" at this point. Callers may continue using their existing string-based calls; when encountering a direction enum, record the original value and inspect Builder's processing result, rather than overwriting it with a custom string first. The requirements for the current implementation are as follows:

Query\Builder::orderBy accepts SortDirection::Ascending and SortDirection::Descending and maps them to 1 and -1 respectively, while asc and desc strings remain supported.

This requirement preserves both the legacy string path and the two explicit direction-enum paths. It does not state that arbitrary objects or arbitrary strings should be accepted. If the observed value is neither `asc` nor `desc`, and is not either of these two enum members, do not infer any other compatibility conclusions from this requirement; preserve the original value and return to the call site to continue checking.

After verifying the direction, proceed to the chunking branch. If the same call both uses a direction enum and enters chunked reading, split the record into two sections: first record the numeric value produced from the direction value, then record the sort objects before and after chunking. Do not delete or rearrange existing sort orders to prove the direction path.

## Current Chunked-Read Replacement

For sort orders used to continue reading, fields must not be appended to the original object indefinitely. The current requirements are as follows:

Chunk pagination removes the previous id alias from MongoDB's associative order map, preserves unrelated secondary orders, and appends the requested id or _id order without numeric-list or stale entries.

When verifying, start with the original associative sort order. First confirm that the previous id alias has been removed from the map; then confirm that secondary sort orders unrelated to pagination still retain their fields and directions; finally confirm that the currently requested `id` or `_id` is present as the pagination field. If the final result becomes a numerically keyed list, it cannot pass, because the field–direction relationship is no longer stored as an associative map. If the final result also contains the old alias, it cannot pass just because the new field appears at the end.

"unrelated secondary orders" refers to other sort entries carried by the original query that are not pagination fields. There may be one, or there may be none. Samples without a secondary sort order can only check removal of the old entry and appending of the new entry; to verify preservation, you must see an actual associative sort order that includes a secondary sort order.

If the original query already contains a sort entry resembling the pagination field, do not delete entries in bulk by name. First identify which entry came from the caller and which came from the previous round of pagination. If you cannot answer that, stop before deleting anything, and save the complete sort order and the field requested this time. This page still does not define any additional marker rules for this issue.

## On-call branches

| Observed form | What to do first | Condition for continuing | Stopping point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The parameter is `asc` or `desc` | Preserve it as is and check the direction after Builder | The original value is still visible | Other code has modified it before it reaches Builder |
| The parameter is a direction enum | Record the enum member, do not manually convert it to a string | The processed direction value is visible | Only the converted temporary string remains |
| The first chunk is correct, but the next chunk is out of order | Obtain the associative sort orders before and after chunking | The old pagination field can be identified | Only the final list is available |
| There is a secondary sort order | Record the field and direction separately | The secondary sort order is still present after rewriting | The secondary sort order has been lost and the original object is unavailable |
| Both `id` and `_id` are present | Mark the stage at which each appears | You can determine which one is the old pagination entry | Guessing their origins based only on their names |
| Duplicate fields or suspected old entries appear | Look back at the object before replacement | The leftover entry can be located | Appending the field again in an attempt to overwrite the result |

A stop in the table does not mean closing the issue or handing off the situation with just the phrase "sorting anomaly". It only prevents continuing to produce inexplicable sort orders when the original object is missing. Recording which item it stopped at and which fields were retained at that point is more useful than outputting another seemingly reasonable trailing sort order.

## Related issues still needing more information

Some reports only say "the order is different after chunk", without the original query or the sort order before chunking. For now, these can only be handled as cases where the original object is missing; the presence of `id` or `_id` in the final result is not enough to prove that the replacement has been completed.

Another issue not yet written up is: if the original query uses field names similar to those used for pagination, how to reliably distinguish the caller's sort from the previous round's pagination entry. The existing requirements only specify that the source must be identified first; no new marking scheme is invented here. When encountering such objects, retain the complete associative sort and request fields, and wait to fill in the details at a point where the source can be identified.

## Legacy appendix: String check quick reference

The quick reference below comes from the earliest records and is only intended to explain the scope of handling at that time, not to serve as current instructions:

```text
- Parameter is asc: continue
- Parameter is desc: continue
- Other parameters: convert to a string, then continue
- Chunking: add id at the end
```

The first two items still explain why legacy string-based calls have not changed; the last two have been superseded by direction enum handling and the requirements for replacing associative sorts, respectively. The appendix is retained because descriptions of old issues often contain only these terms. When citing it, make clear that it reflects the old guidance, rather than rewording the old sentences to make it look as though structural preservation had already been checked at the time.

A current record that can be reviewed can be as short as:

```text
Direction: SortDirection::Descending → -1
Before chunking: priority => -1, id => 1, name => 1
Old pagination entry: id
Current field: _id
After chunking: priority => -1, name => 1, _id => 1
```

This is only a structural example, not a fixed call shape. If there is no secondary sort, state that explicitly; if the old pagination entry cannot be identified, write "unidentified" and stop. Subsequent additions only need to cover actual call shapes, especially scenarios where `id`, `_id`, and a secondary sort appear together.

The `BackedEnum`, `Carbon\CarbonInterface`, `DateTimeInterface`, and `DateTimeZone` at the top of the file are still useful code-reading cues. Earlier notes mistook this proximity for implementation ownership; that conclusion has been withdrawn.

## Preserve the original call forms

Keep migration samples in their original form, in two groups: existing attribute-array calls, and calls that pass a closure in the values position. Array calls do not need to be rewritten as closures for this compatibility round; closures should not be executed first and converted back into arrays just to make inspection easier, either. Only by first sending each group through its original entry point can we tell whether transformations added later changed behavior.

This review uses the following boundary: Eloquent\Builder::firstOrCreate accepts a Closure or array for its values argument without changing the normal attribute-array calling contract.

This does not require all callers to use closures. It only rules out a once-tempting migration step: wrapping a normal attribute array in a closure for "compatibility," or adding another array layer around a closure. Both can make calls look consistent while hiding the original attribute-array calling contract. If you find either of these, first remove the newly added wrappers, then recheck the calls without rewriting them.

The differences between the old checks and the later checks are shown below. The top half is an abandoned sequence and should not be used to set up new samples.

```text
Old checks
Attribute array ──┐
                  ├─ Convert to a similar form first ── Observe results
closure         ──┘

Retained checks
Attribute array ──────────────────────── Recheck independently
closure  ────────────────────────── Recheck independently
```

## The other track: runtime surface

Early Laravel runtime surface cleanup checks only looked at whether the source code had been cleaned up. The stopping criterion then was too permissive: clean-looking source does not establish that the runtime surface has no remnants. This section is retained as a record of the old checks, but is no longer used to determine whether the migration is complete.

The runtime surface needs to be verified in a real CI run, with the job, commit, and actual artifact name from that run recorded. Without those three items, cleanup can only be marked as pending verification; the presence of configuration or static changes cannot substitute for runtime results. Recording progress should not require the closure samples and cleanup to succeed at the same time, either: they share the same compatibility window but have different verification entry points.

## Recovery when issues occur

If a closure sample has problems after migration, first undo any transformations, wrappers, or preprocessing added around that sample and restore its pre-migration call form. Leave attribute-array calls unchanged. Then check whether the issue still appears at the caller or only in runtime-surface checks.

Do not attribute a failure directly to the `DocumentModel` trait. That file can serve as a navigation point on the model side, but it is not the default place to make changes for the work recorded on this page. Places in the old draft that turned "start reading from the trait" into "handle it in the trait" have now been marked obsolete.

Still missing are the full call paths traversed by the closure samples and the actual artifact names for each real run. Supporting material should be attached alongside the specific sample or run record; this page will continue to retain the migration sequence, the withdrawn assumptions, and the scope for restoring the old call forms.

# Collection JSON Compatibility Decision

In the LDA 6.0 compatibility train, Collection JSON schema validation and Optional schema after callback were included in the same regression batch. At this stage, we are not treating this as a shared model lifecycle issue.

Three approaches were discussed: group collection validation and the optional schema after the callback under the same model path; track the two separately and only link them when the same behavior appears; or leave them unclassified for now. The tentative choice is the second.

For collection validation, we first need to determine whether the actual entry point and the sample results are consistent. On the callback side, we need to retain the details of how a missing schema is handled, and compare whether initial processing and repeat processing produce the same content or diagnostics. Both issues can occur in model-related scenarios, but that is not enough to show that the same part of the implementation is responsible for both.
