# Dependency Boundary Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

The initial anomaly was narrow in scope: the same object appeared in different states at two points in time. It was not treated as an ordinary page issue because the object carried the dependency source established by lock, with adoption scope and exit responsibilities linked to it. A state being overwritten could lead someone to believe that the dependency had already switched sources; an expiration action being misread could also trigger an exit decision prematurely. The evidence preserved from the incident does not support these leaps.

The old records included driver capability window, while the current entry point returned a different result. In the first round, no immediate judgment was made about which one was "correct", and the content seen on the two occasions was saved separately instead. That decision continued to hold up later: the state discrepancy was confirmed, but its cause was not. Preserving the incident evidence did not make the issue easier to explain, but at least it did not erase content that could only be seen during a failure.

The first version of the record stopped here. It treated the restoration of grammar alias hook as an important clue and listed changes to atomic reservation as an unknown. At the time, there was not enough evidence to disentangle how the two related to the entry point discrepancy; therefore, the earlier version did not identify a root cause or change the adoption scope. The later work added timing information to these limited facts, rather than retroactively filling in a complete story for the record made at the time.

## Boundaries That Can Still Be Confirmed in This Review

This incident concerns only the dependency boundary audit for Relations. The discussion concerns the dependency sources formed around lock, their adoption scope, and exit responsibilities. It has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. No records indicate that the states of other projects underwent the same change, so the discrepancy between the two environments will not be extrapolated into a cross-project failure.

"The same object" here does not mean two entries with similar names, but the very same object referenced by the audit entry point. Different states at two points in time are enough to require preserving both results; they are not enough to show that the object itself must have been modified. There may have been differences in read conditions, entry point versions, or local state, but these are all possibilities that still need to be investigated and cannot be recorded in the postmortem as changes that actually occurred.

The current entry point returned different revision values at two points in time, which is the most consistent observation on this page. The old records, the recovery page, and the uncertainty about the cause must therefore coexist. They serve different purposes: the old records tell us what understanding guided the handling before the anomaly; the recovery page preserves a usable path; the uncertainty about the cause prevents later readers from forcibly joining the two into a causal chain.

## How the Incident Evidence Was Preserved

The original input and entry point version were preserved first. Further retries were then stopped, not because retrying was necessarily harmful, but because there was not enough information about the request conditions at the time to explain the second read. If continued retries left only new successful results, the most valuable failure state would instead disappear. Stopping at this point also avoided mistaking "what was read later" for "what happened initially".

LMCB-011 later requested that the states before and after the failure be exported. This supplied the comparison missing from the first version: the content before and after the failure could be viewed together, so at least the post-recovery results would not be all that remained. The export did not answer why the change occurred; it merely meant that the state change no longer depended entirely on memory. LMCB-011 also documented an observation that cannot be ignored: the same information about the person on duty produced different expiration actions in the two entry points.

Expiration actions are not decorative fields in this incident. They affect when to continue using something, when to begin phasing it out, and who may adjust the dependency scope based on them. If the expiration actions for two entry points differ, the audit cannot directly write either side back to the other. Even if one user path is restored, that can only prove that path is usable; it cannot replace confirmation of who is responsible for the exit.

The handling of LMCB-008 should likewise be retained. The action is to clear its own cache and rerun once, leaving the shared cache untouched. This put the local cache in a testable position without expanding the incident impact. Once completed, the cold-start comparison had a clear meaning: if the difference disappeared, local state could serve as a possible explanation; if the difference remained, at least the problem could no longer be attributed to an uncleared personal cache.

The existing record points more toward the latter: the two environments continued to produce different current results. The public records for LMCB-005 did not contain a reproduction command, so this is not a difference that has already been repeatedly verified with the same input and under the same conditions. The precise statement that can be retained is "The results differ on the two sides," not "A certain command necessarily causes the two sides to differ." This limitation also explains why no specific invocation or operational detail was recorded at the time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[Original entry point and old records] --> Q{Are the states the same}
    Q -- No --> R[Save the states on both sides separately]
    R --> S[Clear personal cache and rerun]
    S --> T{Does the difference remain}
    T -- Yes --> U[Retain the environment difference]
    T -- No --> V[Record the local cache impact]
    U --> W[Save the recovery path separately]
    W --> X[Do not rewrite the exit determination]
```

The flow in the diagram describes the retention order used at the time, not an automatic remediation plan. It specifically avoids two errors: first, when the states on the two sides are inconsistent, taking the latest result and overwriting the earlier result; second, after seeing one recovery path, immediately changing all dependency determinations to recovered. Both approaches would make it harder to explain anomalies later.

## After the cold start, the problem did not become simpler

After cold-start processing was completed, the personal cache was no longer an unchecked variable. This does not mean that the cache has been ruled out. The records do not provide enough information to say what each of the two environments retained, nor is there a reproducible command for comparing them item by item; therefore, we can only say that the personal cache was cleared and the process rerun as required by the card, not that the cache was unrelated to the difference.

The shared cache was left untouched to avoid introducing a new common change during the preservation period. If the shared cache had also been cleared, even if the two entry points later became consistent, it would be impossible to distinguish whether the state had naturally converged, the cache had had an effect, or a new operation had changed the content visible on both sides. This restraint is not a general troubleshooting rule; it was dictated by the conditions at the time: there were only results from the two sides and no stable command.

The record of the differing results in the two environments was retained in LMCB-005. Initially, someone wanted to supply a command first, then use its output to decide which side to trust; but the command had still not been found at the time. So the response did not stop at saying "the command is missing", but first documented the result discrepancies that could already be confirmed, the entry point versions, and the preservation actions. If reproducible inputs become available later, further comparisons can be added; until then, neither side can be the sole basis for the audit conclusion.

Another boundary in LMCB-005 is single-item updates. After confirmation is received, only the corresponding field is changed, while adj-relations remains in its original state. This is not because the original state has been proven correct, but to prevent unconfirmed differences between environments from spreading through bulk updates. Single-item updates allow subsequent reviews to see which item actually received confirmation and which still remains in the state observed at the time.

## Recovery did not close the incident

The observation that grammar alias hook could be restored was already retained in the first version. It was once treated as a relatively strong clue because recovery occurred after the anomaly; but temporal proximity cannot substitute for causation. Later revisions moved it out of the role of a "possible explanation for the entire anomaly", retaining it as a record that "one path had recovered".

This distinction directly affects how recovery is assessed. If recovery is defined as a particular path becoming available again, then grammar alias hook has met that definition. If recovery is defined as the audit being able to consistently explain dependency provenance, the scope of adoption, and exit responsibilities, then the bar is higher: the states of the two entry points need to be explainable by the same set of retained materials, and the actions at expiration must also no longer contradict one another. The available materials support only the former kind of recovery.

This is also why the recovery page was retained without replacing the old records. It records an available path, not proof that the failure is gone. Treating it as the final state would leave later readers unable to understand why the same object once had two states, or to determine whether recovery occurred at only one entry point. The old records preserve the anomalous aspects, and both should coexist.

Saying that "the last result was green" does not change this. A green result describes only the last observation; it does not explain why the two environments differed, nor can it erase the previously exported failure state. For this incident, the last observation can help determine whether the user path is available, but it cannot, on its own, establish that the dependency boundary has recovered.

## Earlier assessments and retractions

The first version retained the change in atomic reservation as an unconfirmed item. This choice was reasonable at the time: it did coincide with the incident, and there was not enough material to prove it was unrelated. Subsequent review did not uncover any additional direct links, so it can no longer be treated as the leading causal explanation. The old paragraph records the working hypothesis at the time, and retaining it helps explain why the investigation once moved in that direction; from this version onward, it will no longer be used to explain the state discrepancy.

The implicit idea that "once recovery occurs, the states can be synchronized" has also been withdrawn. Recovery happened on one path, while the current results in the two environments still differ, and the actions at expiration are not consistent either. Synchronization would record the unconfirmed side as a definite result, instead making the scope of lock adoption appear clearer than it actually is.

Another approach that was considered but not adopted was to overwrite the old record directly with the current entry point's state. It had an obvious short-term benefit: the page would retain only one state, and users would not see a contradiction. But it would lose the fact that the object had shown different revision values at different entry points, and would also make it impossible to determine later what each pointed to before and after recovery. For dependency boundary auditing, this tidiness is not reliable.

Another approach that was not adopted was to keep retrying until the results on both sides temporarily matched. Without a command for reproduction, this agreement could not establish whether the inputs and conditions were the same; it might merely treat a transient result as a stable state. Therefore, during the incident, unconstrained retries were stopped after the initial save, and subsequent actions were limited to a cold-start comparison, state export, and confirmation of individual items.

These retractions do not mean the original record had no value. The first version accurately preserved the anomaly, the recoverable path, and the unknowns; it did not commit to a root cause. Only after the second version added the card actions could cache handling, environmental differences, and expiration actions be considered together. The third version clarified which related observations were still merely occurring concurrently, and which conclusions could not be inferred from a partial recovery.

## Practical impact on the lock boundary

The dependency source cannot be determined solely from either the old record or the current entry point. When states diverge, the source determination must remain pending confirmation, rather than treating either revision as the default. This will slow adjustments to the adoption scope, but it avoids propagating the result from a single environment as a fact for all consumers.

The adoption scope likewise cannot be determined by "user path recovery". A usable path shows that the path could be traversed at that time; it does not show that other read entry points returned the same state, much less that all adopters were already using the same dependency combination. Scope updates can only be based on the corresponding fields for which confirmation has been received, while unconfirmed items must retain their original state.

Exit responsibilities are most affected by differing expiration actions. If two entry points specify different expiration actions, neither is automatically selected for exit just because it appears to come later or is easier to execute. Both actions and their respective entry points should first be preserved, and then it should be confirmed which action can be used for the current object. The goal here is not to merge the two pieces of information into a neat date, but to avoid an incorrect exit.

The incident did not require rewriting other relation objects, nor was there any material to support expanding the scope in this way. Cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integration involving Query belong to a different problem domain and are not included just because environmental differences appear on this page. DOC-37 documents an approach that was not adopted and can help explain why the dependency audit was not directly changed to a different solution at the time; it does not constitute evidence of this incident's root cause.

## Operational trail left by the card

The completion of LMCB-008 means that one cold-start comparison has already been performed. It does not amount to a conclusion that "clearing the cache alone will fix it". The card explicitly distinguishes between personal and shared caches and retains the condition of clearing only one's own cache. If the comparison is repeated during review, this condition should also be written down, or the results cannot be compared with the original incident conditions.

LMCB-005 After confirmation, only the corresponding field may be changed, while the original state of adj-relations is preserved. This action reflects change-scope control: whichever field the confirmation applies to, only that field is updated; unconfirmed parts do not change along with it. It also avoids disguising environmental differences as a full update.

LMCB-011 focuses on the states before and after failure at the triggered entry point. It does not provide the root cause, but it provides a more useful event boundary than a single screenshot: at least, it shows what was saved on either side of the anomaly. The divergence in expiry actions was exposed during this preservation process and therefore cannot be treated as an unrelated display issue.

The three cards occupy different positions on this page. LMCB-008 describes the cold-start action, LMCB-005 describes how the environment results still differ and the restriction on updating individual items, and LMCB-011 describes the states before and after failure and the differences in expiry actions. Together, they support the approach of "continuing to preserve the discrepancy," but they do not jointly provide a reason sufficient to settle the matter.

## Timeline reordered

For easier follow-up reading, the known sequence is reordered below according to the event relationships, without inventing missing timestamps:

| Order | Recorded content | Impact on assessment |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The old record and the current entry show different states | Preserve both sides first; do not overwrite |
| 2 | Initial observation that the grammar alias hook path can recover | Record it as a local recovery |
| 3 | Reran after the personal cache was cleared; the shared cache was untouched | A limited comparison of the local state was obtained |
| 4 | The two environments still produce different current results | The difference cannot be attributed to the cleared cache |
| 5 | The states before and after failure were exported | Preserve both ends of the change |
| 6 | The two sides provide different expiry actions | Exit responsibility cannot be modified based on only one side's result |
| 7 | The corresponding field can be updated individually after confirmation | The unconfirmed scope retains its original state |

This timeline does not claim that no other operations occurred between the steps. Missing timestamps are still missing, especially the detailed sequence between the first state change and recovery. The purpose of making the sequence explicit is to let reviewers know which observations preceded the later environment records and which judgments emerged only after the cold-start comparison, so that the final, cautious conclusions are not projected back onto the initial incident state.

In terms of impact, the first thing blocked was the audit assessment, not the entire Relations feature. Differences in the driver capability window meant that the old records could not directly answer what the current entry point targeted; the later recovery made one user path usable again, but did not remove the object-consistency requirement for the audit. Therefore, the recovery status on this page has remained "path restored, boundary undetermined", rather than being broadly described as "recovered".

## Checkpoints when reading and comparing

Anyone reviewing this through the archive entry point should first read the original records retained in `docs/adj-relations/incidents/Relations-dependency-boundary-audit-same-object-two-states.md`, then compare the states before and after the failure and the expiration actions on both sides. If only one side is visible, the record should be marked as a one-sided observation; do not use it to rewrite the revision on the other side.

If another cold start is needed, only clear the personal cache and rerun under the known conditions. The existing material does not establish whether the shared cache contributed to the difference; therefore, do not also change it during the review and then compare the results directly with the old records. If the results become consistent after a rerun, record which entry point showed that consistency, rather than immediately deleting the earlier discrepancy.

If explicit confirmation of a field is received, update only the corresponding field within the constraints of LMCB-005. Any parts not covered by the confirmation should remain in their original state. In particular, the scope of adoption and responsibility for exit must not be recalculated as a side effect of updating one field, unless the confirmation itself explicitly covers those judgments.

If a path is restored through grammar alias hook, record it as a local recovery, and do not describe it as the root cause of the dual-state anomaly. If reproducible commands or more complete environment conditions become available later, a section can be added to present the commands, inputs on both sides, and results side by side; until then, the existing material does not support working backward from the recovery to infer the mechanism behind the differences between the two sides.

## Items still unresolved

- As for why the current results differ between the two environments, no reproducible command is available yet.
- Whether the revision values seen at the two entry points come from different read conditions, unconfirmed.
- Which of the different expiration actions can be used for the exit decision, unconfirmed.
- Whether recovery through grammar alias hook depends on a particular entry point version, unconfirmed.
- As for whether the change in atomic reservation is merely a concurrent observation, there is still no direct evidence, but it is no longer the primary line of investigation into the cause.
- For the precise timing of the initial anomaly, cold-start comparison, and local recovery, the records are incomplete.

These questions are retained at the end of the postmortem because they directly determine whether the dependency source, scope of adoption, and responsibility for exit can be pinned down. They are not a substitute for a to-do list, nor do they mean that every issue must be resolved on this page; they are simply the parts of the current incident that cannot be closed with the existing material.

## Conclusion

The recovery that can currently be confirmed is: one path containing the grammar alias hook became usable again at one point. What still cannot be confirmed is: why the same object showed different states at two points in time, why the two environments produce different current results, and which expiry action can support exit responsibility.

Therefore, the dependency sources established by lock will continue to be based on the results retained on both sides, rather than being overridden by a single entry point; the scope of use will be adjusted on an item-by-item basis only after confirmation of the corresponding field is received; exit decisions will continue to retain the expiry actions from both sides until the applicable entry point can be confirmed. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed causes will remain side by side, neither overstating partial recovery as boundary recovery nor removing discrepancies that have yet to be explained.

# Dependency Boundary Exit Window Procedure

This checklist is kept beside relations-supply-boundary's exit window. It checks only the exit action, the last visible result, and adj-relations's exit action; whether the release succeeded is signed off separately by the corresponding owner.

The materials entry point is still `docs/adj-relations/release/relations-supply-boundary-exit-window-checklist.md`. First retrieve the `release evidence bundle` left at the time from that file; do not fill in the window contents based on similar filenames.

## Checks Within the Window

1. [ ] Copy down the last visible result in the bundle and mark the exit action it corresponds to. If only a partial recovery is visible, record the result as a partial recovery; do not record the entire relations-supply as exited based on that.
2. [ ] Starting from the exit action, trace back adj-relations's actual object. Do not use the filename or page color as a basis for the determination; treat the exit action and rollback entry point separately.
3. [ ] Check whether the old value can still serve as the revert entry point. The existence of an old value only shows that rollback is possible; it does not mean the current release is complete.

The old window had an on-site convention: after seeing `document builder`, do not clean up the environment. At the time, this term was used as a reminder to preserve an observation point, not as a completion marker. Then check whether `cache expiry predicate` appears; if it does not, stop here, do not continue cleanup, and do not replace the missing result with speculation.

## Stop and Rollback

If the last visible result cannot be matched to an exit action, stop this check. Keep the bundle and the recorded result, and return to the still-usable old-value entry point; do not combine the rollback state and exit state into one item. If only the rollback entry point can be confirmed, record "Rollback entry point seen, exit not verified".

This checklist covers this window as it was at the time. Leave later branches to the current maintainer; the check order retained here for `document builder` and `cache expiry predicate` may not apply to later windows.

# 6.0 Compatibility Freeze Decision Record

This 6.0 compatibility freeze did not treat the adapter layer as an area that could be overhauled in one go. The dispute centered on the eloquent-model entry point: whether compatibility work should continue through the existing entry point, or whether an adjustment window should be set aside first to reorganize the entry point before starting subsequent stages. A search was carried out using `src/Eloquent/DocumentModel.php` and several related call names; that search only helped anchor the discussion to the same subject, and could not establish the file location as the entry point's permanent home.

What Northstar Data Systems needed at the time was a consolidation point that would allow continued comparison, not a commitment to a future structure. The available materials could identify some surface-level Laravel contracts and call for examining the corresponding MongoDB command or return shape; they did not provide the complete call surface, much less specify which signatures an adjustment window should cover. The meeting therefore compared not "whether refactoring is good," but whether either approach would first erase the very differences the team was trying to find.

## The Two Options on the Table

The first approach was to retain the current entry point. Compatibility behavior that was already observable would still pass through the original path, and new stages would continue in the same cumulative compatibility tree. This way, when a stage went green or showed a local regression, at least the preceding stage would remain available as a basis for comparison; the entry point itself would not simultaneously become another variable.

The cost of this approach was not ignored. Leaving the entry point unchanged would not absorb framework changes on the team's behalf. When a Laravel convention changed, the first sign might be only a local compatibility failure, and it might not be immediately clear whether it involved signature drift, call relationships, or changes to commands and return shapes on the MongoDB side. Those who supported reorganizing the entry point in advance were concerned precisely that this delayed identification would fragment later fixes.

The second approach was to open an adjustment window first. Its supporters believed that if signature differences emerged gradually and the entry point was changed only afterward, observations from the call layer, adapter layer, and compatibility stages could become intertwined. This concern was reasonable; however, none of the materials available at the time could specify the window's starting point, boundaries, or completion criteria. There was also no list of which Laravel contracts should be included together, or which MongoDB commands or return shapes should serve as references.

If the entry point were reorganized under those conditions, even if the compatibility tree later returned to green, it would be impossible to tell whether that green state came from the original contracts still holding or from a newly added bridging layer. A change of unknown scope would alter the observation point first and leave the team to explain the observations afterward. The review therefore did not consider "potentially reducing the pressure of later fixes" a sufficient reason to open the window.

## What Was Actually Decided at the Freeze

The decision was to retain the current eloquent-model entry point and continue only within compatibility stages covered by existing evidence. This was a narrow decision: it did not declare the entry point a permanent boundary, nor did it rule out later adjustments; it simply rejected changing adapters for a hypothetical future call surface before identifying what had drifted.

The order of work recorded at the time was: Escalate framework-signature drift before changing adapters. Here, escalate did not mean attributing every failure directly to the entry point. It meant first making clear which framework signature or Laravel convention had changed, and then discussing whether the adapters needed to follow. Changing the entry point before locating the drift would give the same observation two possible explanations at once.

The materials also contained a more specific constraint: Start from an observable Laravel contract, capture the MongoDB command or return shape, and keep every compatibility stage green in one cumulative tree. This was not a slogan to check off item by item at release time, but the comparison method used in the review. If a surface-level signature changed but the corresponding commands and return shapes could still explain the existing results, the method name alone was not enough to conclude that the entry point had to be reworked. Conversely, if the signature appeared unchanged but the command or return shape no longer matched the original assessment, an unchanged entry point was not a reason to keep giving the go-ahead.

The cumulative tree also had a narrowly defined meaning in this decision. New stages needed to follow the stages that had already been verified; the purpose was to preserve continuous comparison, not to broaden the meaning of a green state into "future Laravel changes are already covered." Speculation not yet tied to a Laravel contract, MongoDB command, or return shape did not gain the same standing as verified stages merely because it sounded relevant to compatibility work.

The review's decision sequence at the time can be condensed into the following path:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Detect a change in a Laravel contract] --> B[Identify framework-signature drift]
    B --> C[Check the MongoDB command or return shape]
    C --> D{Are the subjects sufficiently comparable}
    D -->|Yes| E[Evaluate an adjustment window]
    D -->|No| F[Retain the current entry point]
    E --> G[Integrate into the cumulative compatibility tree]
    F --> G
```

"Retain the current entry point" in the diagram did not mean taking no action. It required subsequent compatibility items to continue starting from observable contracts and to retain the actual shapes as a basis for judgment. "Evaluate an adjustment window" in the diagram did not mean automatic approval either; only when the subjects could already be compared side by side would a window become an engineering option worth discussing.

## Two Variants That Were Not Approved at the Time

The most direct option not adopted was to reorganize the entry point immediately and then fill in the compatibility evidence on the new entry point. Its benefits were speculative: perhaps there would be fewer scattered changes later. Its costs, however, would appear immediately: the entry-point boundary would change, removing a stable comparison surface between the old and new stages. The review did not deny that reorganization might be needed in the future; it simply found that the scope was not sufficiently defined at that moment to explain what this step would actually solve.

There was also a narrower compromise: leave the entry point unchanged for now, but add an abstraction layer in advance, to be swapped out when differences appeared later. This option was also set aside. A placeholder layer without confirmed call targets would add an observation point without reducing uncertainty; the next time results changed, the team would still need to determine whether the change came from a Laravel contract, the old entry point, or the newly added placeholder structure. It did not supply the scope of the affected items, which was what was most lacking at the time.

Objections to retaining the entry point did not disappear once the decision was made. If several observed Laravel contracts later pointed to the same limitation, and the MongoDB command or return shape for each contract could be obtained for side-by-side comparison, a single bounded adjustment might be easier to compare than multiple small fixes. This condition was retained as a reason to reopen the discussion, rather than written into the current freeze.

## Review Notes Added Later

The initial draft placed "keeping the entry point stable" too close to "the compatibility scope can be closed out," making it easy to read as saying that compatibility work would naturally be completed as long as the entry point remained unchanged. That statement later needed to be narrowed. An unchanged entry point only meant changing one fewer variable; it did not prove that the surrounding Laravel contracts had not changed, nor did it prove that the MongoDB side would still produce the same commands or return shapes.

This earlier wording was not removed, because it reflected why the entry point was retained at the freeze; however, it should no longer be read as an overall judgment of adapter stability. The understanding after review was that entry-point stability only provided a basis for comparison. It meant that new observations did not also have to account for the factor that "the entry point has just been replaced," but it could not replace identifying where the observed behavior itself came from.

The use of "the cumulative tree is green" was also reviewed. Previously, some had treated consecutive passes as sufficient reason to keep accepting adjacent changes. The limitation now retained is this: green only means that the stages already included in the sequence could be validated consecutively under the comparison conditions in place at the time. A change not yet tied to a Laravel contract, MongoDB command, or return shape cannot be considered handled simply because the tree is still green.

This did not mean that the original concerns in favor of an adjustment window were wrong. If differences always appeared first as individual regressions, later fixes could indeed end up fragmented. The distinction is that fragmentation is a risk of the approach, not a fact already sufficient to prove that the entry point needs to change. Disagreement over the approach can remain; the items that have drifted and comparable results still have to emerge first.

## Questions Still at the Edges of the Decision

At the time, no finer-grained trigger criteria were established for whether drift should immediately be raised as an entry-point issue if it was first observed outside the entry point while the cumulative compatibility tree remained green. The current inclination is to first record what has drifted and its corresponding shape, then determine whether the entry point needs adjustment. This at least allows the new observations to be placed alongside the comparison conditions from the original freeze, rather than overwriting both with a single change.

If an adjustment window is resubmitted, the materials should identify what is to be adjusted and explain how it corresponds to a Laravel contract, MongoDB command, or return shape. Without these details, the window remains only a proposal and cannot enter the compatibility stages in the name of this freeze. No allocation table for the entry point and all its callers was produced here, nor was every kind of future framework change classified in advance.

DOC-44 are the adjacent handover materials for an offline dependency mirror switch. They can help readers identify another workstream from that time, but cannot replace this decision record on the eloquent-model entry point, the adjustment window, and the reservations.

versions.body:
# Customer Reproduction Intake Discrepancy Postmortem

During the customer reproduction intake window, the visible results did not line up with the customer-provided reproduction description in the way originally planned. Intake itself did not stop, but the staff on duty could not produce a reproduction assessment ready for direct handoff; for materials received during the window, only discrepancies could be flagged at that point, and the original comparison conclusions could not be reused.

When the discrepancy was first noticed, a reflection signature snapshot was retained. It captured the signature shape seen through reflection at the time, not complete proof of adapter behavior. The initial assessment provisionally recorded the issue as "intake used the wrong comparison reference," because the mapping between results and expectations appeared to have broken down. This assessment explained why the adapter was not changed immediately, but there was still not enough material later to establish it as the root cause.

The results visible to intake were then checked again against the original arrangement. The discrepancy remained, and the snapshot was still readable; together, they only showed that an inconsistency had occurred during the window. They did not show that the framework-side signature had necessarily changed, much less establish that the customer materials themselves were error-free. This single observation was not generalized into a problem shared by all reproduction requests.

The temporary recovery was narrowly scoped: results from this window were saved separately from the original arrangement, and intake of reproduction materials continued, but this discrepancy was not allowed to drive an adapter change directly. This restored intake, not a conclusion. If subsequent materials use the original arrangement, the corresponding signature needs to be confirmed again, rather than citing this snapshot as evidence of compatibility.

The control point added in this postmortem is: Escalate framework-signature drift before changing adapters. When there are signs of signature drift, first confirm the drift and escalate it, then discuss adapter changes. This control point addresses the order of actions taken during this window; it does not resolve whether the discrepancy came from the framework signature, the way materials entered the process, or a combination of the two during intake.

This record retains the explanation given at the time that "the wrong comparison reference was used," along with the temporary isolation approach. Recovery took place before the root cause was clear; when the same kind of issue recurs, a new signature snapshot should be saved separately, and the visible results, original arrangement, and isolation actions already taken should each be recorded.

When the ticket says refresh is complete but no verifiable result is available, don't repeat the refresh yet.

```text
Results differ?
├─ relations call entry point and version present
│  └─ For the same input, retrieve the captured MQL command, then compare
└─ Entry point or version missing
   └─ Stop; add these two items first
```
